source_snapshot.message:
feat(mcp): serve Ix tools over MCP, executing commands in-process

Adds `ix mcp`, a stdio MCP server exposing 23 graph tools, so any
MCP-capable client can drive Ix. Each host still needs its own
registration; for Codex that is `codex mcp add ix-memory -- ix mcp`.

Tool calls run inside the server process rather than spawning the CLI per
call. Booting main.js costs ~0.58s before any query runs, which an agent
pays on every hop of a locate -> callers -> read chain; measured end to
end over stdio, eight tool calls drop from 8502ms to 1282ms. It also lets
resolve.ts's per-cwd scope cache survive between calls. Running commands
in the server's own process needs three things the child process gave for
free:

- `ix status` and `ix text` call process.exit(1) on their error paths.
  In a child that ends one command; here it would take the whole server
  down mid-session, so process.exit becomes a throw the runner turns into
  a failed tool result.
- Runs are serialized. Commands report failure via process.exitCode,
  which is a non-configurable property on Node 22 and so cannot be made
  context-local; isolating output per async context while the exit code
  stayed global would attribute a call's output to the right result and
  its success to the wrong one. This costs nothing measurable — three
  concurrent calls as child processes took 1304/1733/1888ms competing for
  Node boots, versus 15/250/251ms serialized in-process.
- The transport writes JSON-RPC through its own handle on fd 1, and
  output that cannot be attributed to a run goes to stderr, so a command
  outliving its timeout cannot desync the protocol. AsyncLocalStorage
  keeps such an orphan's late output out of the next call's result.

The command tree is rebuilt per run because commander does not clear
parsed option values between parses, which would leak --path from one
ix_text call into the next one that omitted it.

IX_MCP_SUBPROCESS=1 restores the isolated child-process behaviour.
